claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially be retained in a high-temperature BCC state by high-temperature treatment followed by rapid quenching.
Phase stability in initially BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by competition between a thermodynamic driving force for chemical ordering and kinetic limitations on diffusion.
Chemical ordering in this alloy is associated with phase partitioning.
Al enhances thermodynamic instability through its influence on chemical bonding.
At lower temperatures, the thermodynamic instability favors transformation from BCC into ordered phases.
Sluggish substitutional diffusion limits the rate and extent of ordering and phase transformation in this multicomponent alloy.
Annealing supplies thermal energy that enables Al and other substitutional species to overcome diffusion barriers, redistribute, and order.
Solute partitioning produces local chemical ordering and nucleation and growth of secondary ordered phases.
Secondary ordered phases may emerge at grain boundaries or within grains.
Within the proposed annealing regime, higher annealing temperatures should produce a larger ordered-phase fraction than the as-quenched BCC baseline.
Longer annealing durations should produce a larger ordered-phase fraction than shorter durations.
Lower-temperature annealing should yield slower or only partial transformation.
Phase-fraction evolution should correlate with diffusion kinetics rather than showing an effectively instantaneous equilibrium transformation.
The proposed mechanism applies in an intermediate thermal regime where diffusion is active but not fast enough to establish immediate equilibrium.
At sufficiently low temperatures, diffusion becomes too slow for appreciable transformation.
At sufficiently high temperatures, the BCC phase is re-stabilized.
Minor compositional heterogeneities could alter local ordering kinetics.
Little or no dependence of ordering on annealing time or temperature, including immediate ordered-phase formation at the lowest temperatures, is designated as a falsifying result.
